claim: A phage-displayed synthetic library for nanobody discovery was constructed in this study.

source: The nanobodies identified were suitable for applications such as immunostaining and immunoblotting, supporting the phage-displayed synthetic library as a versatile platform for nanobody development.

claim: The phage-displayed synthetic library is openly available for non-profit use.

claim: Nanobodies are valuable tools in biological research and therapeutic trials due to their small size, superior stability, and high specificity for target antigens.
source: Nanobodies, single-domain antibody fragments derived from camelid heavy-chain antibodies, are valuable tools in biological research and therapeutic trials due to their small size, superior stability, and high specificity for target antigens (Muyldermans, 2013; Könning et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Nanobodies are ideal for applications beyond traditional in vitro assays, including live-cell imaging and functional studies.
source: These features make nanobodies ideal for applications beyond traditional in vitro assays, including live-cell imaging and functional studies.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nanobody applications.

claim: When fused to fluorescence proteins or functional domains, intracellularly expressed nanobodies enable real-time visualization and manipulation of proteins within living cells.
source: For example, when fused to fluorescence proteins or functional domains, intracellularly expressed nanobodies enable real-time visualization and manipulation of proteins within living cells, providing a useful approach to study cellular dynamics in native environments (Rothbauer et al., 2006; Caussinus et al., 2011; Harmansa and Affolter, 2018; Schnider et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Traditional methods for nanobody generation are limited by immunologic tolerance to conserved antigens.
source: Traditional methods for nanobody generation, which rely on animal immunization, can be costly and time-consuming and are also limited by immunologic tolerance to conserved antigens (Banik et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In vitro technologies such as yeast, phage, and ribosome display have emerged as valuable alternatives for nanobody generation.
source: To overcome these challenges, in vitro technologies such as yeast, phage, and ribosome display have emerged as valuable alternatives, enabling the generation of synthetic nanobody libraries for direct antigen selection without animal immunization (Moutel et al., 2016; Zimmermann et al., 2018; McMahon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The yeast-display platform has proven exceptionally useful for screening nanobodies that recognize distinct conformational states of target proteins.

claim: Drosophila S2 cells were used to produce 8 Drosophila secreted proteins as antigens for nanobody screening.

claim: The positive nanobody-displaying phages could recognize the antigens on the cell surface.

To do this, we incubated the antigen-expressing cells with purified nanobodies, and we observed similar results (Figure 3B), further suggesting that these nanobodies specifically recognize their target proteins.
